vignette:
He is nineteen, a fast food worker on the evening shift, and when he talks about the storm he still calls it "that night," as if naming it more clearly might make it return. Before it happened, his life is ordinary in the way he now misses: school, then work at the restaurant off the highway, coming home smelling like fryer oil, half-listening to his mother remind him to put his uniform straight into the wash. He is single, living with family, saving small amounts from each paycheck without any very clear plan. He describes himself then as someone who did not think much about danger. Weather was weather. Bad things happened somewhere else.

The storm comes in late summer after a day of strange heat. He is at work when customers start coming in talking too loudly, checking their phones, laughing in that nervous way people do when they are trying not to be afraid. The manager keeps everyone on shift because the dinner rush has already started. Through the front windows he watches the sky turn a color he has never seen before, greenish and heavy. Then the power flickers. Someone yells from the kitchen that they should all get away from the glass.

He remembers the sound most clearly. He says it does not sound like wind in movies; it sounds like the whole building tearing open. They crouch in the walk-in cooler, workers pressed shoulder to shoulder with boxes of lettuce and tubs of sauce, while metal rattles overhead and someone prays out loud. His phone keeps vibrating in his pocket with messages from his family, but he cannot make himself look. In those minutes he is certain the roof is going to come down and that he will die there in his work visor and grease-stained shoes. When the noise finally passes, they come out into a restaurant that no longer looks familiar. Glass is blown in. Part of the sign is gone. Outside, power lines sag over the parking lot and cars are scattered at odd angles. He cannot reach his family for hours.

By the time he gets home, parts of the neighborhood are torn apart. Trees are split. One house on the next block is flattened on one side. His family is alive, but he finds them in the dark, shaken and crying, and he feels both overwhelming relief and a strange numbness. In the days after, everyone is busy: clearing debris, waiting in lines for water and ice, charging phones in the car, checking on relatives. He keeps moving because stopping feels dangerous. At night, though, he lies awake listening for sirens, wind, any shift in the air. When rain starts a week later, he gets up and stands by the window, heart pounding hard enough to hurt.

He goes back to work as soon as the restaurant reopens, though even entering the building makes his stomach tighten. The repaired front windows reflect the parking lot, and sometimes he catches his own face there and does not recognize how alert it looks. If a customer drops a tray, he jerks so hard the other workers laugh. He laughs too, embarrassed, but his hands shake afterward. During storms he keeps checking the weather radar on his phone between taking orders. If clouds gather while he is on shift, he feels trapped. More than once he asks to go to the back because standing near the windows makes him dizzy.

Sleep becomes its own problem. He has dreams in which he is back in the cooler, unable to move, hearing the building peel apart. On some mornings his mother tells him he was shouting in his sleep. He starts staying up too late with headphones on, gaming or scrolling until exhaustion knocks him out, because falling asleep feels like stepping toward something that is waiting for him. He wakes already tired and goes to work irritated, snapping at customers in ways he never used to. Then he feels guilty, especially with older people or families with children, and spends the rest of the shift trying too hard to sound cheerful.

His world gets smaller without him fully noticing at first. Friends invite him out, but if the plan involves driving far from home or being anywhere he cannot easily leave, he makes excuses. He does not like being in large stores anymore because the high ceilings and humming lights remind him of the moments before the storm hit. He avoids weather reports but also checks them constantly. When the sky darkens, even a normal summer storm seems personal, like it is aimed at him. He knows, logically, that not every gust of wind means disaster. Logic does not stop his chest from tightening or the image from flashing into his mind of the restaurant windows bowing inward.

He speaks about the version of himself from before the storm as if that boy belongs to someone else. Now he is always scanning, always listening. He sits near exits. He notices where people could hide. At work he volunteers to take trash out only when the weather is clear, and if thunder starts while he is outside, he freezes for a second before running back in, humiliated by how little control he has over his own body. What troubles him most is not only the fear but the sense that the fear has become part of his personality. He wants to feel young and ordinary again. Instead he moves through each day as though something terrible has already begun and he is the only one who can hear it coming.
